profiles.meeting_scenario: A coordination meeting at a fintech company preparing a cross-functional handoff for a technical thought-leadership piece and demo about a new Rust-based concentrated N-dimensional AMM design for stablecoin pools. The context is that Research has finished the core model and Product Marketing is packaging it for an upcoming partner webinar and internal review. The agenda is to align on the interface between the quant/research workstream and the go-to-market workstream: what materials will be delivered, which demo build and charts will be used, what 'risk' and 'hedge' sections are included, and who owns the final shared deck and repo snapshot. The expected outcome is apparent agreement on the deliverables for Thursday's review: a research package, a demo artifact, and slides that both believe are synchronized.

members.name: Nina Rao
members.expertise: AMM design, stablecoin market structure, Rust simulation tooling, quantitative risk framing
members.background: Nina leads a small research team at a digital-asset infrastructure company and previously worked on pricing and simulation tools for multi-asset liquidity systems.
members.private_state: She wants to keep the externally shared material technically credible without exposing unfinished implementation details, and she is worried that marketing will overstate how production-ready the skewed polar-coordinate liquidity feature is.
hidden_assumptions: A 'demo' for this project means the deterministic Rust simulation notebook wrapper and recorded output generated from the internal research branch, not an interactive UI build.
The 'current model' refers to the v0.9 research branch with the latest hedge appendix and revised concentration examples from Monday night.
A 'risk section' should stay scoped to portfolio-level exposure from stacking correlated stablecoin pools and the corresponding hedge intuition, not operational or smart-contract deployment risks.
If materials are marked 'review-ready,' they only need to be internally coherent and technically defensible for the internal Thursday review, even if not polished for external partner viewing.

members.name: Evan Morales
members.expertise: Technical product positioning, webinar packaging, partner communications, cross-team launch coordination
members.background: Evan came from a developer-tools startup and now translates advanced protocol research into collateral for partners, sales engineers, and ecosystem audiences.
members.private_state: He wants a smooth webinar package that looks concrete and near-launch, and he is concerned that overly academic framing will confuse the audience and reduce partner confidence.
hidden_assumptions: A 'demo' means the clickable front-end sandbox connected to the approved staging API, because that is what webinar and partner teams normally show.
The 'current model' is the last shared artifact in the launch folder, namely the v0.8 packaged charts and explainer from last Friday that comms already started editing.
A 'risk section' should cover all risks an external audience may ask about, including pool-stacking exposure, contract readiness caveats, and user-facing implementation constraints.
If materials are 'review-ready,' they should be polished enough that, with minor edits, they can be reused for external webinar rehearsal.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that Nina will send Evan 'the demo' for Thursday.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Nina means a reproducible Rust simulation package with precomputed scenarios showing skewed concentrated liquidity in polar coordinates.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Evan means the staged interactive product-like sandbox that someone can click through during the webinar rehearsal.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In cross-functional business meetings, 'demo' is a routine bridge term that usually feels settled by context; both assume the other naturally uses their department's default meaning and neither expects the need to unpack it.

misalignment_points.topic: Which version is the current model
misalignment_points.surface_form: They repeatedly refer to using 'the current model' and 'the latest charts.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Nina is referring to the internal v0.9 research branch updated Monday night with a new hedge appendix and altered examples for too many stacked stablecoin pools.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Evan is referring to the v0.8 launch-folder package circulated last Friday, because it is the latest version formally shared outside Research.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both versions are recent, both are called 'latest' within their own workflows, and the meeting focuses on coordination rather than version governance, so the phrase sounds precise enough while silently pointing to different artifacts.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree the deck will include 'a risk and hedge section.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Nina assumes this section covers only the quantitative market-structure risk of over-stacking correlated stablecoin pools and the model-based hedge framing.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Evan assumes the section also includes implementation-readiness caveats, integration constraints, and any audience-facing concerns that could arise in partner Q&A.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'risk and hedge section' sounds complete and sensible on its face, and both see themselves as helping the same narrative, but each silently draws the boundary around risks relevant to their own function.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They align on making the materials 'review-ready by Thursday.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Nina believes review-ready means technically accurate enough for internal stakeholders to validate assumptions and identify open questions.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Evan believes review-ready means visually polished and stable enough to flow directly into webinar rehearsal with only cosmetic edits.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Review cycles often use the same milestone label across teams, and because both are discussing a Thursday review, the phrase creates false consensus even though their standards for completeness differ.

I need to make sure nobody treats this as a promise that the feature is production-ready. For Thursday, review-ready just means internally defensible and coherent enough for the review group.
